b: IF (conditional statement!) the only thing we get from our projected investment in AI from 2020–2030 is widespread adoption of Level 5 self-driving cars, then I think it’s not just worth it. It’s an amaze-balls bargain.

For this comparison, I’m using a roughly $6 trillion US AI infrastructure budget across that period, including chips and data centers. And I’m assuming truly autonomous driving becomes widespread: 90% of driving automated, with nobody having to supervise the car.
First, fewer people dying or being injured.

An independent IIHS study found that Waymo had 81% fewer injury crashes per mile than human drivers in the cities studied. That doesn’t establish what nationwide Level 5 driving would achieve, but it gives us something considerably better than just guessing.
So let’s test an 80% reduction in crash harm on automated travel.

Federal crash research, adjusted for inflation, puts the annual harm at roughly $1.7 trillion. That includes death, disability, pain, hospital treatment, damaged vehicles, and lost income. People staying alive and avoiding permanent injuries obviously belong in the calculation.
$1.7 trillion × 90% adoption × 80% less harm = roughly $1.2 trillion in annual benefits.
Americans spend about 95 BILLION hours a year driving. Your commute might still take an hour, but being able to read, sleep, work, or watch something during that hour has value.
Let’s value becoming a passenger instead of a driver at just $5 per hour. That doesn’t mean everyone earns another $5. It means the ability to use that hour differently is worth something.
95 billion hours × 90% adoption × $5 = roughly $430 billion a year.
Combined, that’s around $1.6 trillion in benefits annually once adoption reaches that level.

Now the additional equipment, computing, maintenance, and support won’t be free. For this example, give the system a $600 billion annual allowance for costs ABOVE what our existing transportation system already costs. That’s another assumption, rather than a known price tag.
$1.6 trillion in benefits − $600 billion in additional costs = about $1 trillion in annual net benefits.
Against a roughly $6 trillion initial infrastructure bill.
Under those assumptions, about six years of benefits after widespread adoption would match the investment. And the benefits would keep coming.

Obviously that’s a return to society. It includes people getting to stay alive, people avoiding years of pain, and billions of hours becoming more useful or enjoyable. It isn’t all money appearing in somebody’s checking account.

But if those assumptions hold, self-driving alone could justify the entire infrastructure investment. We wouldn’t need a single additional medical breakthrough, scientific discovery, or productivity improvement to make the numbers work.
And I suspect we’d get a few of those too.
